e-3143.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 \theta = \sec^2{\theta}
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{\color{blue}1+\tan^2 \theta} = \dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{\color{blue}\sec^2 \theta}
$$

We now cancel the common factor of $\sec^2 \theta$ in the numerator and denominator and simplify the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{2\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }}{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{2\sec^2 \theta}{1+\tan^2 \theta} = 2.
$$

e-10053.problem: Express $(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x )$ in terms of $\tan x$ only.
e-10053.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2{x}
$$

First, we expand the parentheses using the difference of squares formula:

$$
(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x ) = 1 - \sec^2x
$$

Then, we rewrite the expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{sec}^{2}⁡x & =1-(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =1-1-{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-{tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(1-\sec x )(1+\sec x )= -\tan^2 x.
$$

e-10052.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression Using the Secant-Tangent and Other Identities
e-10052.problem: Express $2\tan x\cdot(\cot x+\tan{x})$ in terms of $\sec x$ only.
e-10052.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2{x}
$$

Also, recall the following identity:

$$
\cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tan x\cdot \cot x = 1
$$

Using the above identities, we can simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+2{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2\cdot 1+2{tan}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2\text{ }\,(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =2\,{sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
2\tan x\cdot(\cot x+\tan{x})= 2\sec^2x.
$$

First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +{tan}^{3}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \text{ }\,(1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }{\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +{tan}^{3}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }={sec}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sec}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} & =\frac{1-(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{-{tan}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}} \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{1-{sec}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\,({sec}^{2}⁡x-2{tan}^{2}⁡x) & ={cos}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\,(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x-2{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the identities:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},\,{cos}^{2}⁡x=1-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

 

Using the above identities, we can further simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\cancel{{cos}^{2}⁡x}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\,({sec}^{2}⁡x-2{tan}^{2}⁡x)=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.

after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the secant-tangent identity:

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We rewrite the given expression using the secant-tangent identity as follows:

$$
\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }=\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }
$$

We now simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{sec}^{2}}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }
$$

 

Using the above identity, we can further simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$
